analysis.one_liner: Strips the funding used to enforce stricter tailpipe pollution limits on new cars.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted the bill down 52-46 on April 18, 2024, falling short of the 60 votes the floor agreement required, so the EPA rule survived.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar any fiscal year 2024 federal money from being used to carry out the EPA's rule setting stricter greenhouse gas and smog-forming pollution limits for new cars and small trucks, including any similar rule. The standards would phase in for model years 2027 through 2032. The bill failed a Senate vote that required 60 votes in favor; it got 52.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle manufacturers and the oil industry, because the bill would relieve them of the compliance costs and gasoline-demand pressure created by stricter emissions limits for new vehicles.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits FY2024 funds from being used to implement, administer, or enforce the EPA's Multi-Pollutant Emissions Standards rule for light-duty and medium-duty vehicles, or any substantially similar rule.
By defunding enforcement, the bill would spare automakers the cost of meeting stricter tailpipe limits for greenhouse gases and other pollutants during the 2027-2032 phase-in.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, who would face looser tailpipe limits on the pollutants that drive smog and climate change for every new car sold, and future buyers who lose the fuel savings those standards are designed to produce.

drawbacks.text: Blocking the rule would leave weaker tailpipe limits on greenhouse gases and criteria pollutants for light- and medium-duty vehicles sold through model year 2032.
The bill is narrow: it only cuts off fiscal year 2024 funds, so even if enacted it would not permanently stop the EPA from administering the rule, only hobble it for that year.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that stricter emissions standards can raise the upfront price of new vehicles, and the bill offered that price relief by giving up the pollution reductions and fuel savings the rule was designed to deliver.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Any near-term savings in vehicle compliance costs would come at the expense of dirtier air and higher greenhouse gas emissions from a fleet of millions of vehicles over more than a decade. On top of that, the bill's one-year funding cut would not cleanly repeal anything, just obstruct enforcement, making it a poor tool even for people who oppose the rule.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate brought the bill up under an agreement that required 60 votes to pass it; it got only 52 and failed.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Crapo introduced the bill on March 23, 2024, and it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate took up the bill on April 18, 2024, and it failed by a 52-46 roll call because the governing order required 60 affirmative votes.
The vote split almost entirely by party: 48 of 49 Republicans voted yes, while 44 of 48 Democrats and 2 of 3 Independents voted no; 3 Democrats and 1 Independent voted yes.

The EPA's multi-pollutant rule, which the bill targeted, sets stricter standards for greenhouse gases and criteria pollutants for light- and medium-duty vehicles phasing in over model years 2027 through 2032.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people are better off because the bill died: the stricter tailpipe standards stand. The vehicle manufacturers and oil interests that pushed for the rollback got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

for.name: 3 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 3 Independents
for.what_they_did: Voted yes, breaking with their party.

sides.party_line_note: Nearly every Republican (48 of 49) voted yes and nearly every Democrat and Independent (46 of 51) voted no, with 3 Democrats and 1 Independent crossing over to yes.

industries.note: The bill would lift the compliance burden of stricter tailpipe standards for model years 2027-2032, and their interest in avoiding that cost ran directly against the public's interest in cleaner air and lower emissions. It failed, so they keep the standards.

Stricter emissions standards push new vehicles toward cleaner engines, which cuts gasoline demand over time; defunding the rule would slow that shift and preserve fuel sales. The bill failed, so the rule remains in place.

industries.industry: Electric vehicle and charging infrastructure suppliers
industries.note: Slowing the emissions phase-in would slow demand growth for electric vehicles and charging, which depends on the same transition the standards drive. The bill failed, so this loss did not happen.
